title: Shvetaketu Comes Home
hook: a son comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows it all, and his father asks one question he can't answer
carry: after the doing comes the wish to know brahman
tomorrow: Bhrigu asks his father what Brahman is. why won't his father just say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Mimamsa: arthavada, the fire that wept silver, and stories that praise the act being asked for.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Veda. At twenty-four he comes back. He's learned all of it, the hymns, the rites, and he walks in, as the text puts it, full of himself, sure he's learned. His father, Uddalaka, lets him settle. Then he asks one question. Did you ask your teachers for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `HOME, FULL OF HIMSELF.` → `ONE QUESTION HE CAN'T ANSWER.`

segments.voice: So Uddalaka shows him. Know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay. The pot and the bowl are just names, shapes, words. What's real is the clay. Shvetaketu is stunned. My teachers can't have known this, he says, or they'd have told me. Please, you tell me. And the father begins the teaching we'll hear more of this week: underneath everything there is one reality, which the Upanishads call Brahman. That's Vedanta, the Veda's end, the teaching of the Upanishads. Its root text, the Brahma Sutra, opens with one short line: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. The great commentators stop on its first word. Now, after what? Shankara says: after a person learns to tell the lasting from the passing, cools toward rewards, gathers calm, and longs to be free. Ramanuja says: after the study of ritual, the earlier inquiry. Two readings, kept side by side. Either way, the teaching is plain. In Hinduism, doing the rites well is not the end of the road. A day comes when a person who has kept the fasts and lit the lamps asks what all of it rests on. That wish is honored, not suspected. It's where Vedanta begins. Shvetaketu didn't lose his twelve years. He finally asked what they were for.
screen: `KNOW THE CLAY, KNOW EVERY POT.` · `ONE REALITY: BRAHMAN.` · `NOW, AFTER WHAT? TWO READINGS.` · `THE RITES AREN'T THE END.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you do out of habit or faith, a prayer, a fast, a lamp, a way you greet your elders, and do it in your mind, step by step. Then let one quiet question rise: what does this rest on? Don't answer it. Hold the wish to know, the way Shvetaketu finally did. If you pray, you can ask it in the presence of the One you pray to.
Vedanta. The Veda's end, the teaching of the Upanishads, which opens with the wish to know Brahman, the one reality under everything. Today's word.
Your line: after the doing comes the wish to know Brahman. Like Shvetaketu, ask what it all rests on. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Students of Vedanta traditionally begin the Brahma Sutra with its first line, the wish to know Brahman, read through their lineage's commentary, often Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the Chandogya's story of Shvetaketu is one of the best-known ways the Upanishads are taught.

fork.reveal: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. like Shvetaketu, the question comes after the doing, and it's honored.

Brahman.meaning: the one reality under everything, in Vedanta

Shvetaketu.meaning: the son who came home proud from twelve years of study

Uddalaka.meaning: Shvetaketu's father and teacher in the Chandogya

Shankara.meaning: a Vedanta commentator who reads now as after inner readiness

Ramanuja.meaning: a Vedanta commentator who reads now as after ritual study

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 (Shvetaketu leaves at twelve, returns at twenty-four proud; the teaching by which the unheard is heard; the clay, its names and its reality; 'my teachers cannot have known this')
Brahma Sutra 1.1.1 (now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.1 (what the 'now' follows: discernment, dispassion, calm and the rest, longing for freedom)
Ramanuja, Shri Bhashya 1.1.1 (the 'now' follows the knowledge of ritual works)
